title: ‘The Mummy’ Poster Ads Banned From London Underground After Advertising Watchdog Cites ‘Distressing’ Imagery
description: The U.K. Advertising Standards Authority has ruled that outdoor poster ads for “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” breached its code by presenting an image tha
body:
The U.K. Advertising Standards Authority has ruled that outdoor poster ads for “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” breached its code by presenting an image that gave “a realistic impression of a dead child,” while clearing companion TV and streaming spots for the same campaign.

	The ASA investigated four issues stemming from several complaints about ads for the Warner Bros Entertainment U.K. Ltd. cinema release, seen in April this year. The regulator upheld one complaint and rejected the other three in a ruling published Aug. 5.
	

	“The ASA received 30 complaints, many of whom believed the ads were distressing for children and adults,” the ASA said.


	Posters on the London Underground and at outdoor sites showed a close-up of a mummified female figure with grey, ashen skin, cracked lips and one eye swollen shut, wrapped in material resembling a shroud and inscribed with hieroglyphic-style symbols.

	The ASA said the figure’s features gave “a realistic impression of a dead child” and that the material wrapped around her added to that impression. Because the posters ran in untargeted locations, including on the London Underground and at a site visible from a children’s nursery, the regulator concluded the imagery was likely to distress young children who saw it. It ruled the posters unsuitable for outdoor display in that form, finding them in breach of CAP Code rules 1.3 and 4.2.

	Warner Bros. had argued the poster’s neutral expression, open eye and absence of a sarcophagus or restraints were deliberate choices meant to reduce distress, and noted the studio’s outdoor buying policy of keeping horror titles at least 100 metres from schools – a standard that does not extend to nurseries.
	

	The ASA ordered that the poster ads “must not appear in the form complained of” and directed Warner Bros. to keep future marketing likely to frighten young children away from places where they would see it.

	The ruling cited BCAP Code rules 1.2, 4.1, 4.10, 5.1 and 32.3, and CAP Code (Edition 12) rules 1.3, 4.1 and 4.2.

	The ASA rejected a separate complaint that the posters trivialized child loss or ongoing global conflicts, finding that text identifying the image as promotion for a film provided sufficient context, even if some viewers found it distasteful.

	Variety has reached out to Warner Bros. Discovery for comment.

	The campaign also included a TV ad and a matching Prime Video ad depicting a family receiving a call about a daughter who had gone missing eight years earlier, with the father questioning what she was doing in a 3000-year-old sarcophagus. On-screen text read, “Some Things Are Meant to Stay Buried.” Both ran with a post-7:30 p.m. scheduling restriction cleared by Clearcast.

	The ASA found the TV and streaming ads were unlikely to cause serious distress and that their scheduling restrictions were sufficient to limit exposure to young children, rejecting complaints that they should have been kept off air later or targeted more precisely on Prime Video. It also noted Clearcast’s data showing an average children’s index of 31 across the TV placements – well below the industry baseline of 100 that represents typical child viewership, indicating the actual child audience was low. No further action was required for the TV and streaming ads.

	“Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” released in the U.K. on April 17 and grossed $2.9 million.

schema.headline: ‘The Mummy’ Poster Ads Banned From London Underground After Advertising Watchdog Cites ‘Distressing’ Imagery

title: Alba Rohrwacher-Starrer ‘A Common Story’ Gets Boarded by True Colours Ahead of its Venice and Toronto Premieres (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Italian sales company True Colours has taken world sales outside Italy on first-time director Anna Foglietta’s marriage drama “A Common Story” (“Una
body:
Italian sales company True Colours has taken world sales outside Italy on first-time director Anna Foglietta’s marriage drama “A Common Story” (“Una Storia”) starring Alba Rohrwacher, ahead of its bow in Venice and Toronto.

	Foglietta is an actress-turned director best-known to international audiences for her role in Italy’s smash hit “Perfect Strangers” that earned her a David di Donatello nomination. She also served as the official emcee of the 77th Venice International Film Festival.
	

	“Common Story” is the tale of Erika, played by Rohrwacher – whose credits include Pablo Larraín’s “Maria” and who served on the 2025 Cannes competition jury panel – and Mauro, played by Guido Caprino (“The Art of Joy”) whose simple life in the countryside is disrupted when their daughter Irene leaves to go to university abroad. Their house feels empty, and the balance on which this couple had based their lives seems to crumble. “This profound, intimate crisis will push them to really look at one another and understand if and how they can transform themselves and, consequently, their love,” says the synopsis.


	“Common Story” will world premiere in September at Venice’s Horizons section, followed by a North-American launch in Toronto’s Discovery section.

	Foglietta’s directorial debut is produced by Italy’s HT Film, Indigo Film, Tenderstories and Blu One Lab with support from RAI Cinema and HBO Max also on board. BIM Distribuzione will release the film in Italy.

	“This marks the beginning of an international journey we’re proud to embark on with True Colours, which shares our faith in a film that, thanks to its author’s vision, manages to delve with extraordinary sensitivity into the depths of everyday life,” said HT Film’s Viola Prestieri.
	

	Commented True Colours chief Elliot Gustin: “For the past 10 years, True Colours has consistently worked to discover and promote new Italian filmmakers. Anna is clearly one of the most talented voices of her generation and, with ‘A Common Story,’ she succeeds in portraying the crisis faced by a couple and a woman with great tenderness and sensitivity.”

	“We are delighted to be supporting this unique new female voice around the world, starting with the Venice and Toronto film festivals,” he added.

	Other titles on True Colours’ 2026 slate comprise Dario Albertini’s family drama “Armony,” starring Valerio Mastandrea and Asia Argento, that is launching from Locarno’s Piazza Grande; Susanna Nicchiarelli’s upcoming “Happy Days” with Riccardo Scamarcio (“Modì”) and Carlotta Gamba (“Portobello”); and Paolo Civati’s doc “Masters” which portrays nine prominent filmmakers including Jane Campion, Tim Burton, and Martin Scorsese.

title: Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+
description:
Disney is going long on short-form content.

	The entertainment giant struck an alliance with TikTok that will have creators on the popular quick-hi
body:
Disney is going long on short-form content.

	The entertainment giant struck an alliance with TikTok that will have creators on the popular quick-hit video service making shorts tied to characters and stories from Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars, FX and more. The resulting pieces from creators who opt-in to the program will be available on both TikTok and on Disney+ in the form of “Verts,” the company’s vertical video products. 


	“This collaboration creates a new bridge between the stories we tell and the creativity they inspire, giving creators a bigger stage to share what they’ve made, and audiences more to discover on Disney+ every day,” said Asad Ayaz, Disney’s chief marketing and brand officer, in a statement. 
	

	The agreement will launch in the U.S. in coming months, and the companies intend to move it to other markets around the world. Financial terms were not disclosed.

	It’s no secret that younger people are watching shorter videos with more frequency, including TikTok vignettes, Facebook Reels, even “whip-around” sports shows like NBC Olympics’ Gold Zone and NFL Red Zone. The format is driving conversations around everything from wellness to food to pop culture. Many prominent advertisers are also investing in it, with big-spending companies including Procter & Gamble and JCPenney creating “microdramas” and “microcontent.”

	Disney has telegraphed its interest for months. It already introduced “Verts” to ESPN’s direct-to-consumer streaming service, and unveiled plans for short-form video to surface on Disney+. “Short form and creative content, they’ve exploded in the past few years, and it’s an area we’re focused on because we have deeply committed fans who, you know, love our brands and our franchises and characters, and they want to engage with them in this new way,” said Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro, speaking during a May call with investors. “This is specifically important when we think about Gen Alpha, obviously, the newest generation of Disney fans. What we’re doing is we’re experimenting with short-form content in a variety of ways.”
	

	The TikTok alliance might fill in for a previous ambitious project that was ultimately scrapped. Disney in December unveiled a three-year deal with OpenAI that would have allowed users of the company’s generative-video Sora platform to generate short, user-prompted social videos using a set of more than 200 masked, animated or creature characters from Disney, Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars, as well as costumes, props and vehicles. Disney planned to make a $1 billion equity investment in OpenAI, and receive warrants to purchase additional equity.

	The project, however, was ultimately scrapped after OpenAI decided to shut Sora down.

	Now TikTok will help Disney move further into the emerging field. Both companies will administer a “Disney Creator Ambassador Program” that will give certain users incentives and access to events and career development.  TikTok creators will gain access to assets related to hundreds of films and series from Disney’s vast library, and fans will be able to take part in a Disney-centered experience on TikTok  that will be refreshed regularly.

	“Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful,” said Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok, in a statement.

	There is some hope that allowing Disney intellectual property to fuel TikTok pieces will have a halo effect for Disney’s films and programs. Nearly half of respondents on a survey commissioned by TikTok and conducted by Ipsos, a market-research firm, said that discovering entertainment content on TikTok spurred them to go on to watch a movie or show on a streaming service or traditional TV.

	In January 2026, under a deal brokered by the Trump administration, ByteDance sold a majority stake in TikTok’s U.S. business to non-Chinese investors, including Oracle, Silver Lake and Abu Dhabi’s state-owned investment firm MGX. Beijing-based ByteDance retains 19.9% of the joint venture; the deal brought ByteDance and TikTok into compliance with the U.S.’s TikTok divest-or-ban law that went into effect in January 2025.

schema.headline: Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+

title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review
description: Anyone with even the vaguest understanding of the profit motive can understand why Apple TV sports comedy “Ted Lasso” has returned three years after
body:
Anyone with even the vaguest understanding of the profit motive can understand why Apple TV sports comedy “Ted Lasso” has returned three years after its poorly received — yet still widely watched — third season seemed to close the book on its story. A streaming service continuing to milk one of its few major hits doesn’t prohibit the result from being enjoyable; if the first three seasons of “Ted Lasso” are effectively one (overlong, especially toward the end) sports movie, then Season 4 is its perfectly routine sequel. And in a genre filled with redemptive second chances, “Ted Lasso” could use one of its own. If a show has the chance to correct for mistakes like overindulgence and bloat, why not take it?
	

	Season 4 introduces a premise that gives Jason Sudeikis’ titular American-football-turned-British-football coach a chance at both a fresh start and a return to old stomping grounds. Two years after Ted walked away from AFC Richmond and took his signature mustache back to Kansas City, team owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), marketing chief Keeley (Juno Temple) and operations head Leslie Higgins (Jeremy Swift) arrive stateside with an offer he can’t refuse: coaching the club’s brand-new women’s team, who begin their existence as the underdogs — specifically, Greyhounds — their male counterparts once were. Given the cultural bias against women’s sports leagues, they’ll likely remain so even if they succeed.


	The concepts of class reunion (Ted goes back to London and gets the gang back together!) and clean slate (Ted takes on a new challenge!) are somewhat at odds. Sure enough, Season 4 is far more enjoyable as the latter than the former — even as “Ted Lasso” keeps privileging nostalgia and tired subplots over its best chance at a renaissance. Tanya Reynolds of “Sex Education” is a welcome addition as Alice Chilton, a coach whose constant scowl and clipped severity make her a well-suited foil for Ted’s sunny optimism until she inevitably warms to it. But, at least in the five episodes provided to critics out of an eventual 10, she’s pretty much the only new character who feels fully established, because “Ted Lasso” refuses to make room in the ensemble by sidelining (or is it touchlining?) old ones.
	

	Like Sudeikis, actor Brett Goldstein remains a creative force behind the camera, which may explain why his churlish then player, now coach Roy Kent remains such a presence despite the pivot away from his men’s squad. But while foregrounding Rebecca and Keeley makes sense given the renewed focus on women in sports, Roy and Keeley’s on-again, off-again romance lost its allure several seasons ago. Figures like Roy and Ted’s longtime deputy Beard (series co-creator Brendan Hunt) would be better deployed as occasional cameos, yet they remain load-bearing — and space-occupying — protagonists. The consequences can border on the absurd: a major decision by Ted’s ex-wife Michelle (Andrea Anders) is sped through rather than shown from her perspective; an episode hinges on a team problem with cliques that’s only depicted onscreen far too late. Until then, we’re mostly told about it by other characters with longer tenures.

	Contributing to the sense of overcrowding is an otherwise welcome development: no single episode of the first five clocks in at over an hour, the way so much of Season 3 did. “Ted Lasso” is not for everyone; the blindingly earnest social consciousness and relentless positivity some find so grating remain firmly in place. (Feminist commentary was never the series’ strong suit, and centering the women’s team prompts more of it than ever.) But Season 4 reigns in some excesses and offers glimpses of fresh new faces: a walk-on player who’s also a single mom; a goalie who refuses to wear gloves; a new mentor for Rebecca, played by comic legend Tracey Ullmann. If only the show would clear the field for them.

schema.headline: ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review

title: What Sponsors Actually Get for Their Millions in Sports Partnerships
description:

	A few mon
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	A few months ago, crowds lined the 18th green at The Riviera Country Club in Pacific Palisades, California, as 26-year-old American golfer Jacob Bridgeman secured his first PGA Tour victory at the 2026 Genesis Invitational. But the tournament wasn’t just drawing golf fans. Around the course, guests wandered through hospitality lounges, sampled Korean-inspired food and beverages, explored the latest Genesis vehicles and settled in to watch the action from premium viewing areas.
	

	Genesis may have cornered the golfing market, but their activation at recent events is the kind of experience that’s becoming increasingly common across sports. Today’s biggest sponsorships are about far more than logos on a leaderboard or a name on a tournament. Brands are creating experiences that bring consumers into the action, turning fans into customers long before they ever make a purchase.


	T-Mobile, for example, has expanded its sports strategy well beyond traditional sponsorships. The company helps power everything from broadcasting to on-site operations at sporting events. But for fans, the partnership is experienced in more tangible ways: discounted tickets, access to exclusive Club Magenta lounges at events like the PGA Championship and other member-only perks that make for long-term

	Luxury automakers are taking a similar approach. Mercedes-Benz, for example, has built a strong connection with consumers through Formula 1, where the sport’s focus on performance, engineering and innovation naturally aligns with the brand’s identity. For newer luxury brands, sports sponsorships can serve as a powerful way to start building the recognition that legacy brands already have.
	

	Genesis entered that same competitive space in 2015 as a new luxury automaker. Without the history of its established rivals, the brand looked to sports—particularly golf—as a way to create deeper connections with consumers.

	Why golf?

	The sport offered a natural overlap with the audience Genesis wanted to reach, their executives tell Variety, from business leaders and global travelers, to luxury consumers who value premium experiences.

	As the first Official Vehicle and Mobility Sponsor of the PGA Tour, Genesis has embedded itself into events including the Genesis Invitational, Genesis Scottish Open and as well as emerging made-for-TV formats like TGL. The strategy has coincided with rapid growth, with the brand surpassing 1 million global vehicle sales and reaching a record 82,331 U.S. vehicles sold in 2025.

	The decision to commit to golf early in the brand’s journey was intentional, according to Jose Munoz, President and CEO of Hyundai and Genesis Motor North America.

	“At the beginning, partnering with the PGA Tour and with Tiger—and committing to golf consistently—was a big decision for us,” Munoz tells Variety. “Back then, we were selling just a few thousand vehicles, and today we’ve achieved record sales and significant growth. We cannot be happier with everything we’ve done together, and the partnership has become not just strategic, but also personal.”

	That long-term approach is perhaps most evident in the experience Genesis has built around its tournaments.

	Drawing from the Korean concept of sonnim, or treating guests as honored visitors rather than customers, the brand has reimagined hospitality as more than traditional VIP access. At events like the Genesis Invitational, that philosophy comes to life through thoughtfully designed lounges, elevated food and beverage offerings and welcoming spaces that encourage guests to linger rather than simply pass through.

	That philosophy carries into the vehicle itself.

	I spent a week behind the wheel of the Genesis GV70 SUV, and those same priorities showed up in the details. On a long drive from Savannah to Augusta, the driver’s seat massage function became a small but memorable touch that made hours on the road feel effortless. Combined with customizable mood lighting, a quiet cabin and technology that felt intuitive rather than distracting, the experience reflected the same attention to comfort and hospitality I’d seen throughout the tournament.
	

	It reinforced something I hadn’t considered before: the sponsorship isn’t just about putting Genesis in front of consumers—it’s about creating a consistent brand experience wherever someone encounters it. Whether that’s relaxing in a hospitality lounge overlooking the 18th green or settling in for a four-hour drive, the feeling is intentionally the same.

	Across industries, more brands are recognizing that familiarity is one of the most valuable assets they can build. The companies that stand out aren’t always the ones with the longest history—they’re the ones that consistently create experiences people remember.
	
		Genesis Fan Shop	

	Genesis is not just showing up at events — the brand is also partnering with brands on must-have merch and apparel that’s become as coveted as a seat behind the wheel. Here’s a look at a few pieces available to buy online now.

title: ‘The Blacklist Was a Plague’ — Locarno Retrospective Curator Ehsan Khoshbakht Talks About What We Can Learn From the Intolerance of the Past
description: One of the most shameful episodes in Hollywood’s history is being examined in a new retrospective to screen at the Locarno Film Festival: Red & Blac
body:
One of the most shameful episodes in Hollywood’s history is being examined in a new retrospective to screen at the Locarno Film Festival: Red & Black: Hollywood Left and the Blacklist. Speaking to Variety, the retrospective’s curator, Ehsan Khoshbakht, speaks about the inspiration for the program, which features the work of directors, writers and stars such as John Garfield, Joseph Losey, Dalton Trumbo, Dorothy Parker, Richard Wright and Charles Chaplin.
	

	What was your starting point for the retrospective?

	I have often wondered why someone who could have lived a life of comfort would instead fight for the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War, as the screenwriter Alvah Bessie did. Or why filmmakers such as Joseph Losey and Cy Endfield at the height of their success would leave their families, and end up working in Mexico, England or Italy, often forbidden even to use their real names. Trying to understand that inner compulsion — not to name names — became the starting point.




	

					‘España otra vez’ written by Alvah Bessie
									Courtesy of Mercury Films
	



	Did you see contemporary resonance in your program?

	My reaction was to intolerance and hysteria in the arts. This is not a right-versus-left program. It’s about what happens when the media are abused and misused; when smear campaigns and fear-mongering prevail over rationality and dialogue. There were films such as “Salt of the Earth,” whose Mexican actress was forcibly removed by immigration officers in the middle of production and deported. The blacklist caused serious health problems, tore families apart, drove people to suicide, and prevented some potentially great films from ever being made. It was a plague.
	

	So, it is a bitter irony that 80 years later, Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment the other day. Is it ever going to stop? Every film in the program responds in some way to one of the ugly excesses of the world now, and to the destructive policies of the current administration in the U.S. I didn’t select the program according to that criterion. It is just a painful and frightening coincidence.

	How did exile change the way the filmmakers worked?

	They were forced to adapt to filmmaking modes and industries that were alien, smaller and less streamlined. This introduced what I see as a brilliantly eclectic combination of European style and taste with American sensibility and dynamism. Losey’s “Stranger on the Prowl,” with its unusual and effective blend of neorealism and the man-on-the-run theme, is one example among many. Jules Dassin explored his previously unexamined fascination with the psychosexual. Both filmmakers went on to contribute to a modern cinematic language that could not have developed in America. Others, like Bernard Vorhaus, simply crashed out.



	

					‘Mission to Moscow’ by Michael Curtiz
									Courtesy of BFI/Warner Bros.
	



	What films are you particularly excited about?

	I’m excited about some of the films for various reasons: some because they are key blacklist films that hadn’t been screened before, even in major retrospectives. For instance, the pro-Soviet and frankly embarrassing “Mission to Moscow,” which is a Hollywood film that depicts Stalin as a fair-minded, brilliant leader!

	Then there are some films that haven’t been screened in this particular context, such as “España otra vez,” the first Spanish film made under the Franco dictatorship to deal explicitly with the Spanish Civil War from the point of view of the defeated side — the Republicans. It’s in the program because it was written by and starred one of the Hollywood Ten, Alvah Bessie. 



	

					‘The Intimate Stranger’ 
									Courtesy of BFI
	



	Another super-rare film is “The Intimate Stranger,” by Joseph Losey. Perhaps, the most self-conscious meditation on the blacklist. This film was impossible to show for decades. Losey’s son, Gavrik, will be in Locarno to introduce it. There are nearly thirty 35mm prints in the program, and for some of them to be seen in original format is a chance of a lifetime.
	

	The retrospective seems to hold a special place of esteem in Locarno among festival-goers.

	Other contemporary festivals allocate their worst venues to classic films, if they show them at all. Locarno gives us their best venue, the superb GranRex. I cannot think of any other film festival in the world that would allow me to select 50 titles — mostly in 35mm prints — edit a book of newly commissioned essays by leading scholars from around the world, and produce a podcast. I think it matters to our director, Giona Nazzaro, to go deeper into the history of cinema. He’s an avid cinephile.

	As for our partners, UCLA Film & TV Archive, Cinémathèque suisse and the BFI have all provided us with essential support.

	This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

	The 79th Locarno Film Festival runs over August 5-15.

schema.headline: ‘The Blacklist Was a Plague’ — Locarno Retrospective Curator Ehsan Khoshbakht Talks About What We Can Learn From the Intolerance of the Past

title: Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation
description: Local police were dispatched to the Miami home of Hollywood gossip journalist Perez Hilton after receiving reports about a disturbing livestream dur
body:
Local police were dispatched to the Miami home of Hollywood gossip journalist Perez Hilton after receiving reports about a disturbing livestream during which Hilton, covered in blood, appeared to be cutting himself, Variety has confirmed.

	The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office received multiple calls about Hilton’s livestream on Tuesday night and sent deputies to respond. Once on scene, officers spoke with several of Hilton’s family members. Authorities confirmed that Hilton was alone in his home during the time of the live stream. Deputies have since been ordered to “tactically disengage,” but continue to keep an eye on the situation.
	

	The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office also confirmed that Hilton was safely transported from his home to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention.  


	“In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritize de-escalation by creating time, distance, and opportunities for communication,” the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said in a statement. “Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimize the risk of injury to the individual, deputies, and the public.”

	“We are aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton. At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him. Our primary concern is Perez’s health and well being, as well as the well being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further,” Golden Artists Entertainment CoCEO’s Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan said in a statement when Variety reached out for comment. “We appreciate everyone’s concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time.”
	

	Hilton launched his career in the early 2000s, operating a popular celebrity gossip blog that offered a biting, unfiltered look at some of Hollywood’s most unsavory moments. In a 2012 sit-down with The New York Times, Hilton said that he was no longer aligned with his provocative reporting.

	“What’s important for me is not being liked, but it is that people think I am no longer toxic to the world,” he said. Hilton later added, “I’m aware of the fact there are going to be a lot of people with lingering resentment and a lot of skeptics.”

schema.headline: Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation

title: Eli Roth Admits ‘Ice Cream Man’ Features AI-Assisted Shots After Suggesting Otherwise: ‘I Misspoke’
description: Eli Roth first promised that his upcoming horror release, “Ice Cream Man,” would feature an animated sequence he had initially drawn himself. Now, d
body:
Eli Roth first promised that his upcoming horror release, “Ice Cream Man,” would feature an animated sequence he had initially drawn himself. Now, days ahead of the film’s Aug. 7 premiere, Roth admitted AI had a hand in the effort.

	The horror director said in a statement on Tuesday (via Polygon) that he used AI in “a very small portion of a few scenes in the film” after social media posts claimed the technology was used abundantly throughout the film and pointed to the involvement of the AI visual effects studio Dark Half. 
	

	The statement came after Roth detailed a sequence in the film to Polygon that features a cartoon that seemingly hypnotizes children, turning them into murderers. Roth said he initially drew the animated portions himself, inspired by a 1920s-era Mickey Mouse cartoon of the character parading through a haunted house, before he had animators “help kind of make it a little more fluid” and an artist gave it “an old-timey jittery feel.”


	“I misspoke,” Roth said in a new statement Tuesday. “AI was used in a very small portion of a few scenes in the film. It was an opportunity where technology and creativity came together to help bring my vision for the film to life.”

	Representatives for Roth and Dark Half did not respond to Variety‘s initial request for comment. The revelation is the latest example of how engaging the technology — and obfuscating such use — can roil audiences eager to support new films. 

	“Late Night with the Devil” directors Cameron and Colin Cairne had to explain their use of AI after the version of the 2023 horror film that debuted in theaters featured multiple AI-generated images, while “Stop That Train” director Adam Shankman claimed that the RuPaul-led film featured “ZERO shots conceived by AI in the movie” and that every shot in the film was made by “human hands” after social media users took issue with the employment of Ryan Kavanaugh’s Acme AI and FX firm.

schema.headline: Eli Roth Admits ‘Ice Cream Man’ Features AI-Assisted Shots After Suggesting Otherwise: ‘I Misspoke’

title: Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes
description: Magic realist love story “Chapa 100,” absurdist political allegory “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and cross-continental queer drama “Hibiscus by the Riv
body:
Magic realist love story “Chapa 100,” absurdist political allegory “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and cross-continental queer drama “Hibiscus by the River” look like some of the potential standouts at Locarno’s talent-deep, wide-ranging 2026 Africa-focused Open Doors, unspooling on-site at Locarno over Aug. 5-10.

	Winner of a 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award no less, moving from observational social realism to – literally –  flowering magical realism, love story “Chapa 100” is set in Mozambique capital Maputo. It marks scribe-helmer Ique Langa’s follow-up to “The Prophet,” a 2026 IFF Rotterdam main competition entry.   
	

	Beginning with an impossible snowfall blanketing a drought-ridden Ugandan village, “A Vineyard for a Lobster” signals the feature debut of Ugandan Talemwa Pius, a New York Film Academy alum.


	Now in advanced development, “Hibiscus in the River” is one of five projects brought to market at Locarno by David Ikeata at Vox Cinematic Films, a burgeoning force on Nigeria’s new film scene. 

	Screenings this year at Open Doors pack a particularly powerful punch taking in, for example, Suzannah Mirghani’s Venice Critics’ Week premiere “Cotton Queen,” a Thessaloniki’s best film and Doha Audience Award winner and the first feature-length fiction film from Sudan that is written and directed by a woman. 

	Also on show is “Crocodile,” a doc-feature best film, Viewpoints laureate at Tribeca Film Festival, New York and Youth Jury Prize at the U.K.’s Sheffield DocFest, and “Diya,” a 2025 TIFF Centerpiece title praised by those who caught it. 
	

	Aymar Esse’s touching “My Father’s Kora” world premieres at Locarno. 

	A Snapshot of Africa’s Upscale Film Scene

	Carefully curated, Open Doors 2026 provides a telling take of the range of current upscale titles coming out of Africa plus their artistic and industrial trends. 

	Though light years from parity in Africa at large, women cineastes feature prominently at Open Doors, dominating its producers, new Open Doors Connect and directors sections. 

	Also, “the cohort of Open Doors 2026 is made up of projects and filmmakers that don’t compromise with authenticity,” says Suzsi Bankuti, head of Open Doors. Many titles are indeed redolently and proudly local. “I Live in V.I’s” “character ensemble and dramatic situations are colored with different aspects of the Nigerian collective psyche,” promises director Ugochukwu Azuya. 

	In “Crocodile,” Nigeria’s The Critics collective, though achieving increasing global renown, debate what it takes to be a Nigerian filmmaker.

	Directly or indirectly, most films deal with the state of Africa today. That includes a critique of post-colonial dynamics. Formally, the British Empire et al. has gone. But their legacy lingers. In “Cotton Queen,” set on a Sudanese cotton farm, teen Nafisa, raised on her grandmother’s heroic tales of battling British colonizers, sets out to save the cotton fields – and herself when a British businessman arrives planning to introduce genetically engineered cotton.

	“‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ grows out of my interest in how colonial structures continue to shape authority, belief and communal life in Uganda decades after independence,” explains director Talemwa Pius.

	Facing Africa’s Challenges

	It Takes a Village, a panel at Locarno Pro on Aug. 8, will examine new investment cinema models. Africa desperately needs them, crippled by a fundamental lack of traditional national film funding incentives. Open Doors does hint, however, at some ways African cinema can go and indeed is going. 

	One is the full international co-production and sales agent route, empowering a production with top technical talent. One case in point: Produced by Caroline Daube’s Strange Bird in Germany and Didar Maneki’s Maneki Films in France and co-produced by Annemarie Jacir’s Philistine Films in Palestine and Jordan, “Cotton Queen” was set up as a Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Sudan production, supported by 10 institutions in those countries and Netherlands’ Hubert Bals Fund.  
	

	African companies are not just looking towards Europe, however. At Locarno’s mass networking encounter Match Me!, Amadeu Alban at Brazil’s Movioca is currently in development on two Brazil-Nigeria projects, “Trapped” and “La Pyramide,” reflecting his strategy of building co-productions across the Global South.

	Or filmmakers are turning to genre, with its ingrained entertainment drive. Brought to Open Doors by producer Tapiwa Chipfupa, “Life On the Other Side of the Sun” has supernatural elements; “Diya” weighs in as a blood money crime thriller. 

	Pius uses genre storytelling “to reclaim African narratives and expand how the continent is represented on screen,” he says. Open Doors producer David Ikeata’s slate at Vox Cinematic Films spans “fiction and genre-driven storytelling,” he notes. 

	Rather than a market ploy, however, that passion can come from the filmmakers themselves. “Crocodile” charts how Godwin and Raymond, not yet 11, create a homemade collective with siblings and cousins, shooting ever more ambitious sci-fi films on one of their dad’s iPhones.  

	Or companies can seek out larger same-territory entities, galvanized by global streamer deals. Nemsia Studios, one of Nigeria’s leading film production-financing companies which signed a slate deal with Prime Video in 2022, has boarded Ikeata’s “Hibiscus by the River” as a financing partner. 

	Such deals may be for the lucky few. Their tenor is clear, however. A new initiative, Open Doors Connect, bringing together producers from Africa, Latin America and Asia, aims “to move co-production, circulation and long-term collaboration beyond traditional industry schemes,” Bankuti says. Larger collaboration, now being essayed by film industries as established as France and the Nordic States, is the bigger major way Africa’s film industries can also go. 

	Open Doors 2026 Selection

	Open Doors 2026 is focused on African projects, producers and directors from outside the northern Maghreb and Egypt and South Africa.

	Open Doors Projects

	“Accept My Plea for Burial” (“Baryo Aas Iga Gudoon,” Mohammed Sheikh, Djibouti, Somalia, Qatar)

	After Warmooge, 12, falls to his death while playing with Waasuge, a fellow goatherd, the village elder fails to resolve the case via customary law and religious counsel. From Minnesota-based U.S.-Somali filmmaker Sheik’s follow-up to “Barni,” screening at Locarno, “a morally complex story where there is no clear truth, told through a rarely seen Somali cultural framework,” he says.
	



	

					‘Chapa 100’
									Ique Langa
	



	“Chapa 100” (Ique Langa, Mozambique, Portugal)

	Sitóe, 80, a Maputo flower vendor, and Valentina, a widowed vegetable seller, fall in love. When he is killed by a speeding minibus when trying to help her, flowers begin to bloom within the vehicle. “My love letter to Maputo, ‘Chapa 100’ is ultimately a story about love, memory, and the invisible bonds that connect us and to the places we call home,” Langa tells Variety.



	

					‘I Live in V.I’
	



	“I Live in V.I” (Ugochukwu Azuya, Nigeria)

	One of the first titles from Lagos-based Ensemble, launched by Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola last year, a social class satire from Azuya, whose short ghost story “Swimming in a Sea of Trauma,” played IFF Rotterdam. Florence, 23, to avoid a tough commute to her job in luxurious Victoria Island, squats in an abandoned high-rise, a relic from an ‘80s government building project. “A film about grief, urban alienation and gentrification in the city of Lagos exploring the lost hope of the Nigerian dream,” say Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola. 

	“The Ones With the Tempered Flowers” (Neema Ngelime, Tanzania)

	Ngelime’s debut feature, a diary-like essay, she says, using constructed archives, cinema verité performances with her family and stop motion to explore, respectively, Neema’s 1990s childhood, today and imagined future. An auto doc feature about “a journey I am taking,” “exploring identity and the expectations of womanhood,” says Ngelime. Produced by LBx Africa, run by creative producer Bramwel Iro and director-producer Sam Soko.

	“Too Much Music” (Aseye Fiagbe, Ghana)

	A music doc bio, about Kiki Gyan, a Ghanaian keyboard prodigy catapulted to international fame as a teen with Afro-rock pioneers Osibisa, which he left over conflict over credit and ownership. Shaping African disco and funk, but unrecognised, he became famed for addiction and an early death. “Kiki’s story is about memory and erasure, about who gets remembered for their work and who is remembered only for how they fell,” says Fiagbe.



	

					‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’
	



	“A Vineyard for a Lobster” (Talemwa Pius. Uganda)

	Billed as absurdist political allegory, after mysterious snowfall blankets a drought-stricken Ugandan village, a desperate trader, a disgraced priest and a reluctant chairman exploit the “miracle.” Their escalating ambitions threaten to tear the community apart. From Kampala-based Gripmagic, “in the film, an impossible snowfall in a Ugandan village becomes a political allegory, echoing colonial intrusion,” says Pius.  
	

	Producers

	Tapiwa Chipfupa, Ambidextrous Pictures, Zimbabwe, “Life on the Other Side of the Sun”

	Heading Ambidextrous, founder of AVEL and Girls Making Films training programs and a producer exploring “implications of tradition, culture and custom within modern-day Zimbabwe and on the continent, particularly in the life of women,” says Chipfupa. One case in point:“Life On the Other Side of the Sun, ” a supernatural thriller set in a men-ruled mountain hamlet which slides into desperation and witch hunts – until the free-spirited girl Sungano emerges as the village heroine.

	Natasha Craveiro, Korikaxoru Films, Cabo Verde, White Mask (“dja branku dja”) 

	“In a market dominated by advertising, we established an auteur cinema production house as an act of resistance and cultural affirmation,” Craveiro says of Korikaxoru Films, set up in 2017. Following on multi-prized docu-fiction fest fave Pirinha (2024), she is now developing hybrid feature “White Mask” which plumbs what she calls her father’s “identity denial:” “a Black man from Cabo Verde who served as a soldier in the Portuguese army and, after the war, erased his Cabo Verdean life to settle in Portugal as a judge.”

	David Ikeata, Vox Cinematic Films, Nigeria, “Hibiscus by the River”

	Set up in 2024 by Nigerian actor Chimezie Imo and producer David Ikeata, Vox Cinematic Films slate includes “Hibiscus by the River,” the tale of a young Nigerian man who moves to England to pursue an education, only to find himself pulled back into the currents of his past. Holmes Awa, behind Prime Video’s “Soft Love,” directs. South African producer-screenwriter Paballo Molingoane, and Bulgaria’s U.K.-based Teodora Shaleva also produce.

	Mamounata Nikièma, Pilumpiku Production, Burkina Faso

	General secretary of the Africadoc Association Burkina over 2009-2014 and honored at the Pan-African Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou, Africa’s largest cinema festival, in 2021. Behind multiple doc-features, such as “Djeliya, Memory of Mandingo,” an ambitious, five-county co-pro. “Our vision is to become a national and continental reference in film production, digital marketing, and promotion, championing impactful African storytelling, creating jobs for professionals, and nurturing emerging talent,” Nikièma has said.   
	

	Rua Osman, Helomur Picture, Sudan, “Manageable Matter”

	Osman’s Helomur focuses on stories that explore memory, identity and social transformation, while fostering meaningful South–South and international co-productions. At Locarno with 

	her “Manageable Matter,” a film take on Berlin-based Emma Waltraud Howes’ installation, staging a procession of the Paradox Crew as an Artichoke Brigade, feature nine performances. These build a “meditation on repetition, collective endurance and the search for humility and grace within seemingly unresolvable cycles,” the synopsis reads. 

	Adja Soro (Studio KÄ, Ivory Coast, “Unchosen”)

	Behind Abidjan’s animation Studio KÄ and now Studi KÄ France and editor-in-chief of Spark Anim and developing African stories such as YA animated thriller series “Unchosen.” It turns on Esmel, an Olympic taekwondo silver medal winner who returns home a national hero, but, linked to his father’s unsolved murder, risks everything in a live TV interview, to help him find his missing sister. “Through Esmel’s journey, ‘Unchosen’ explores the violence of public exposure in a world where the line between good and evil grows thinner every day,” says Soro.

	Open Doors Feature Screenings 

	“Barni” (Mohammed Sheik, U.S., Somalia)

	Sheik’s debut feature, a 2025 Red Sea Fest competition world premiere line-produced by Kadir Harbi at Minneapolis-based Aleel, now behind “Accept My Plea for Burial.” Sheik’s passion to depict Somalia through a Somali lens plus older generation fecklessness shines through as Amini leaves her somnolent village to find sis Barni, 9, in a big city. Arrestingly shot – whether ochre scrub-desert or a big city scrap yard beach –  speaking well of Sheik/Harbi’s larger production ambitions.

	“Catcher” (aka “Wrestlers,” Derhwa Kasunzu, Burkina Faso, France, Democratic Republic of Congo, Saudi Arabia)

	When Kelekele Lituka, a wrestler who became world champion in 1974, dies in 2021, he’s buried with little fanfare. To honor him, the New Generation wrestling club announces one last catch event in his honor, despite a war-torn Kisangani and the fact its members are getting on in years…. A “lovingly made film,” said an IDFA description. 
	



	

					‘Cotton Queen’
	



	“Cotton Queen” (Suzannah Mirghani, Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan)

	An undoubted Open Doors standout, sparking some rave reviews – “a beguiling mix of magic-realist fable, coming-of-age drama and post-colonial critique,” says Eye for Eye – scoring top plaudits at a slew of festivals labs such as Cannes’ Cinéfondation L’Atelier and sales from Totem Films to MAD Solutions/Film Clinic Indie Distribution (Arab-speaking countries), TAPE Collective (U.K./Ireland) and Jip Film (Germany). Cotton Queen “highlights how Sudanese girls must navigate authority in all its forms, whether patriarchal or matriarchal – from the specter of colonialism, to familial authoritarianism to the needs of contemporary capitalism,” Mirghani has said.

	“Crocodile” (The Critics, Pietra Brettkelly, New Zealand, Nigeria)

	Built on footage collected by The Critics, a kids’ collective filmed over 13 years through 2025 as Godwin, Raymond, not yet 11, launch The Critics, a filmmaking collective based out of a hardscrabble part of Kaduna, Nigeria, making sci-fi and super-hero films. Now, still determined to make Nigerian genre, they’ve received a digital camera from J.J. Abrams and Morgan Freeman’s narrated Ogun Ola: War Is Coming.” “Crocodile” The Critics and New Zealand’s Brettkelly, whose “A “Flickering Truth” played Venice and TIFF and “Yellow Is Forbidden” Tribeca, chronicle together that journey. 

	“Diya” (Achille Ronaïmou, Chad, France, Germany, Ivory Coast)

	Rated by critics who have caught it – TIFF’s in-house review calls it “a relentless thriller” – “Diya” sees Dane, an NGO driver, accidentally knock down and kills a child, whose family demands an exorbitant blood debt – a diya – driving Dane ever deeper into crime. Ronaïmou’s feature debut, a critique of diya, still widely extended in Chad, in a film praised for its moral complexity, engrossing tension and sense of place. Bought by Canal+ and a triple winner at the Brussels Intl. Film Festival.   



	

					‘My Father’s Kora’
	



	“My Father’s Kora” (“La Kora de mon père,”Aymar Esse, Benin, Switzerland, Germany)

	A Locarno world premiere. Souleymane, an Afro-German trans man, talented fashion designer and increasingly less timid figure on Berlin’s ballroom scene, travels to Dakar to repair his father’s kora. In doing so, he repairs himself, building his new identity rooted in part in his origins, his griot family in Dakar. Souleymane’s journey’s is sluiced by simple but touching scenes such as his bonding with his brother sewing and with grandfather praying and metaphorical shots of the wash of the ocean on Dakar’s beaches.       
	

	“The Prophet” (“O Profeta,” Ique Langa, Mozambique, South Africa, Qatar)

	Preaching in the village of Manjacaze, his inspiration and congregation dwindling, evangelical Pastor Hélder turns to black magic to fire up his oratory and heal his parishioners. His powers come at ever larger sacrifice, literally. Pointedly framed, even in vertical box aspect, bringing sense and sensitivity to shots, a black and white film parable becoming “an expression of the community [Manjacaze] that inspired it,” marking out Luque as a director to track.

	“Katanga: the Dance of the Scorpions” (“Katanga la danse des scorpions, Dani Kouyaté, Burkina Faso)

	Last caught by Variety at Abidjan’s SICA, debating African cinema’s future, here vet Kouyaté (“Sia, the Dream of the Python”) re-imagines “Macbeth” in Africa, shot in bold black and white and placed in a broadly modern setting. A Fespaco Yennega Etalon d’Or winner, creating many new scenes, but key plot beats and the broad parable of overweening ambition remain.

schema.headline: Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes

title: ESPN Taps Creators to Help Promote the NFL Season and its First Super Bowl Telecast
description: ESPN has lined up its fourth annual “Creator Network” of digital stars who will fan out across the country to promote the 2026 NFL season that is se
body:
ESPN has lined up its fourth annual “Creator Network” of digital stars who will fan out across the country to promote the 2026 NFL season that is set to culminate with the Super Bowl airing on ESPN for the first time.

	The five members of the cohort for this year are, as described by ESPN:

	Chase Murman (@theQBplug) TikTok | Instagram | YouTube — Founder of The QB Plug, one of social media’s fastest-growing football brands, known for original quarterback storytelling and athlete-first content that has helped redefine how the next generation consumes football.
	

	Isaac Rochell TikTok | Instagram | YouTube — Former NFL defensive lineman, sports media personality, and creator who combines an authentic player’s perspective with relatable storytelling around sports, fatherhood, and life beyond football.


	Simone Scott TikTok | Instagram — Sports creator, host, and reporter who makes football, basketball, and other sports approachable through clear, engaging content that helps fans better understand the games and storylines driving the conversation.

	Diana Flores TikTok | Instagram — Captain and quarterback of Mexico’s World Champion National Flag Football Team, global ambassador for the sport, and bilingual creator helping grow flag football’s reach ahead of its Olympic debut at LA28.

	Leah Cammarano TikTok — Sports analytics creator and former Carolina Panthers Football Analytics intern who makes advanced football data accessible through engaging, easy-to-understand storytelling.

	“This is a major moment in ESPN’s history, and we have an incredible opportunity to tell that story in new and authentic ways,” said Kaitee Daley, ESPN’s senior VP digital, social and streaming content. “Partnering with creators who have built passionate communities through their distinctive voices and storytelling styles will help bring fans closer to the people, culture and highlights that will define the road to ESPN’s first Super Bowl.”
	

	ESPN first established its Creator Network in 2022 as the cable giant sought to embrace new forms of content and promotion for its game coverage and studio shows. The 2026 group will be given broad access to attend college football games, NFL events including the upcoming Super Bowl set for Feb. 14 at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium. ESPN and ABC will share the rights to the big game, marking the return of pro football to ABC’s air, some 20 years after the “Monday Night Football” franchise shifted from ABC to ESPN.

	ESPN is one of many blue-chip media brands that have worked to harness the power of buzzy creators to produce social media and video content. In the sports context, NBCUniversal brought influencers and creators to help drive conversation around the Milan Cortina Winter Olympics in Italy. In February, the NBA enlisted more than 200 creators to help promote the NBA All-Star Game and All-Star Week events in Los Angeles.

	ESPN’s Creator Network is supported by Blue Hour Studios, a social media-focused brand and media strategy agency based in New York.

title: Perez Hilton Sparks Police Response After Alarming TikTok Livestream in Miami-Dade
description:
Perez Hilton
                          Cops Respond to Miami Home Amid Alarming Livestream
body:
Perez Hilton
                          Cops Respond to Miami Home Amid Alarming Livestream
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 4, 2026
                            7:32 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 4, 2026
                                9:00 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
            8/4/2026 8:53 PM PST -- The Miami-Dade PIO tells TMZ ... The individual has been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention.
      
    
            The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office Crisis Response Unit and Licensed Mental Health Professionals are also on scene providing support and resources to the individual’s family.
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
            8/4/2026 8:00 PM PST -- Golden Artists Entertainment Co-CEOs Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan tell TMZ ... We are aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton.
      
    
            At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him. Our primary concern is Perez's health and well-being, as well as the well-being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further.
      
    
            We appreciate everyone's concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time.
      
    
            Perez Hilton was at the center of a police response in Miami-Dade after authorities received reports he was livestreaming alarming behavior, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Alarming video from Perez’s TikTok Live appeared to show him bloodied while visibly distressed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office tells TMZ ... deputies received multiple calls about the livestream and quickly located the male's residence.
      

            Deputies spoke with family members at the scene, who confirmed the male was alone inside the home.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Authorities say deputies have since “tactically disengaged” but continue to monitor the situation.
      
    
            Perez rose to fame in the early 2000s through his celebrity gossip website and later became a television personality known for covering Hollywood’s biggest stars and scandals. He is the father of 3 young kids.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We’ve reached out to Perez, his representatives and family members for information about his condition ... so far, no word back.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.

title: Perez Hilton: Ambulance Seen Transporting Man Outside His Home Following Frightening Livestream
description:

                          Ambulance Seen Leaving His Home After Alarming Livestream
body:
Perez Hilton
                          Ambulance Seen Leaving His Home After Alarming Livestream
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 4, 2026
                            9:22 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A man believed to be Perez Hilton has been transported to a nearby hospital after deputies rushed to his Miami home, following multiple reports that someone inside was live-streaming acts of self-harm on social media, TMZ has learned.
      
    
      
      UPDATE: A person believed to be Perez Hilton has been taken from his Miami home into an ambulance following a reported self-harm incident.Miami-Dade authorities earlier responded after multiple calls about a livestream, spoke with family, and monitored the situation while… https://t.co/gvuZEbc4ea
              @TheNewsTrending
  
    
            Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office PIO tells TMZ ... "The individual has been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention."
      
    
            The PIO adds, "The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office Crisis Response Unit and Licensed Mental Health Professionals are also on scene providing support and resources to the individual's family."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office deputies and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews descended on the home in the Westchester neighborhood after receiving numerous emergency calls.
      
    
            Neighbors at the scene told NBC6 they believed the person inside was celebrity entertainment blogger Perez Hilton. Law enforcement has not officially confirmed the individual's identity.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to dispatch audio obtained by TMZ, the patient was described as a 48-year-old male who may have ingested multiple prescription medications and was self harming.
      
    
            As we previously reported, deputies responded after "receiving multiple calls regarding an individual who was live-streaming acts of self-harm on social media." Authorities said the person was alone inside the residence when they arrived.
      
    
            Rather than forcing an immediate confrontation, we're told authorities used crisis intervention techniques while working to de-escalate the situation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The standoff eventually came to an end when paramedics were seen wheeling an individual out of the home on a stretcher before loading them into an awaiting ambulance.
      
    
            Authorities have not released the person's condition or provided additional details about what led up to the incident. The investigation remains ongoing.

title: Diddy's Prison Release Date Pushed Back After Fight Behind Bars
description:
Diddy
                          Release Date Pushed After Prison Fight
body:
Diddy
                          Release Date Pushed After Prison Fight
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 4, 2026
                
                            3:42 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 4, 2026
                                4:19 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Diddy's prison release date was just pushed back after the brawl he got in behind bars.
      
    
            According to the Federal Bureau of Prisons ... Diddy now won't get out until February 20, 2028. This comes just days after his release date had been moved up from February to January.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The scandalized music mogul's release date had been jumping around a bunch lately -- it was originally slated for summer before jumping up to April, then February, then January ... and now back to February.
      

        
                    
                  
      
    
            It's not clear why the date had been moving up so much.
      
    
            The January release was even set after Diddy was thrown into solitary confinement for his prison fight -- but now they're walking back the January release, and it's unclear what their reasoning is. 
      
    
            He was sentenced to 50 months in prison after his conviction on two prostitution charges back in October 2025.

title: 'A Toxic Love Story' Leslie Breaks Silence, Says Filmmakers Pulled Bait and Switch
description:
'A Toxic Love Story' Leslie
                          Doc Screwed Over Ian, Made Me a Fool
body:
'A Toxic Love Story' Leslie
                          Doc Screwed Over Ian, Made Me a Fool
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 5, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ian Diaz's best friend Leslie is disgusted by the outcome of "A Toxic Love Story" ... accusing the folks behind the Netflix documentary of pulling a fast one by making her look like a lovesick dope.
      
    
            Here's the deal ... Leslie became a lightning rod for trolls who say she's blind to Ian's crimes because she's madly in love -- even though he's in the slammer for a cyberstalking plot involving his former wife Angela Connell Diaz and ex-girlfriend Michelle Hadley.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Now, Leslie's slamming filmmakers for making her come off that way ... insisting she never should've trusted them.
      
    
            Leslie tells TMZ ... "I expected them to do the research on all they heard from all those filmed for this doc. They were given so much information -- and then decided to abort the truth and ignore all the actual evidence."
      
    
            Adding insult to injury -- Leslie claims the doc crew did her dirty by only using a short snippet of a two-day interview ... just to have a cop from the investigation that targeted Ian dismiss her meager contribution as coming from a lovesick fool.
      
    
            She also says the narrative that Ian refused to participate in the doc needs some serious nuance. She says he was down -- but filmmakers allegedly wanted to interview him over a series of phone calls. Ian wasn't willing to burn through his allotted prison phone time because he's got a wife and kid, so it was scrapped.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As for the haters and trolls ... Leslie couldn't care less about the keyboard warriors -- she still completely supports Ian, telling us ... "If this documentary would've given a robust report of the actual evidence involved in his conviction, more people would be speaking about the inconsistencies and the flat-out agenda to put him behind bars."
      
    
            As we reported ... Leslie was among those who wrote emotional letters to the judge, asking for leniency when Ian was ultimately sentenced to a decade behind bars.
      
    
            We reached out to Netflix ... so far, no word back.
